questions.stem: What is a drug's nonproprietary (generic) name meant to do?
questions.why: The nonproprietary/generic name exists to avoid duplication — giving each drug one standardized name regardless of who manufactures it.

options.t: A name describing the drug's exact chemical structure
options.why: A full chemical structure description is the chemical name's role, not the generic name's.

options.t: A name that only applies outside of the United States
options.why: Generic naming isn't restricted to non-US markets.

options.t: A name chosen by the manufacturer mainly to help market the drug
options.why: Marketing is the role of the brand/trade name, not the generic one.

options.t: A single name meant to avoid duplication across drugs

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a brand (trade) name?
questions.why: The brand or trade name is chosen by the manufacturer for marketing purposes.

options.t: A name giving the drug's precise chemical structure
options.why: Chemical structure description is the chemical name's function, not the brand name's.

options.t: A name the manufacturer chooses purely for marketing
A name used mainly within scientific research papers
options.why: Research contexts typically use generic or chemical names, not brand names.

options.t: A name meant to prevent duplication across drug names
options.why: Preventing duplication is the generic name's role, not the brand name's.

questions.stem: What is tall man lettering used for?
questions.why: Tall man lettering capitalizes distinguishing letters (like DOBUTamine vs. DOPamine) to help prevent medication errors between similarly spelled drug names.

options.t: Marking a drug as a federally controlled substance
options.why: Controlled substance status is marked differently, not through tall man lettering.

options.t: Flagging the pediatric version of an adult drug
options.why: Tall man lettering isn't used to distinguish pediatric from adult formulations.

options.t: Marking that a particular drug needs to be kept refrigerated at all times
options.why: Refrigeration requirements are indicated separately, not through this lettering convention.

options.t: Highlighting the difference between similar drug names

questions.stem: What is a semisynthetic medication?
questions.why: Semisynthetic medications start from natural sources — plant, animal, or mineral — and are then chemically modified in a lab.

options.t: Harvested straight from a plant with no processing
options.why: No chemical processing at all describes a purely natural extract, not semisynthetic.

options.t: Made from natural sources, then modified chemically
A term that only applies to controlled substances
options.why: This term isn't restricted to controlled substances specifically.

options.t: Made completely from scratch with no natural source
options.why: Made completely in a lab with no natural source describes a fully synthetic drug, not semisynthetic.

questions.stem: On the DEA's controlled substance schedule, what does Schedule I represent?
questions.why: Schedule I represents the highest potential for abuse and no accepted medical purpose — the most tightly restricted category.

options.t: A category reserved for over-the-counter products
options.why: Over-the-counter medications generally aren't scheduled controlled substances at all.

options.t: The lowest potential for abuse of any scheduled drug category
options.why: Lowest abuse potential describes Schedule V, the opposite end of the scale.

options.t: Highest abuse potential, no accepted medical use
A category carrying no prescribing restrictions
options.why: Scheduled substances carry restrictions by definition — Schedule I is the most restricted.

questions.stem: What additional security measures apply to controlled substances?
questions.why: Controlled substances require additional security including double-lock storage, extra record keeping, and specific disposal precautions.

options.t: A second provider must witness every dose that is drawn
options.why: Witnessed waste is common practice, but the requirements that define controlled-substance handling are double-lock storage, extra records, and disposal rules.

options.t: A written physician order is required before every single dose
options.why: Standing orders cover many controlled-substance administrations; the distinguishing requirements are storage, records, and disposal.

options.t: Double-lock storage, extra records, and disposal rules
Only a requirement that the drug stay refrigerated
options.why: Refrigeration is a stability requirement for a handful of drugs, unrelated to a substance's controlled schedule.

questions.stem: What is the first step of medication processing in the body?
questions.why: Absorption is the first step — getting the drug from its route of administration into the systemic circulation.

options.t: Biotransformation, occurring later in the process
options.why: Biotransformation is the third step, occurring later.

options.t: Absorption, the very first pharmacokinetic step
Distribution, which is actually the second step
options.why: Distribution is the second step, occurring after absorption.

options.t: Elimination, the fourth and final step overall
options.why: Elimination is the fourth and final step of this process.

questions.stem: What happens during the distribution step of pharmacokinetics?
questions.why: Distribution is the drug's ability to spread through the body, shaped by medicine factors (size, ability to bind or dissolve) and patient factors (fat, water, protein content).

options.t: Spreading through the body, shaped by drug and body factors
A chemical change the drug undergoes in the body, typically in the liver
options.why: A chemical change in the liver describes biotransformation, the step after distribution.

options.t: The kidneys filtering the drug out of the body
options.why: Kidney filtering describes elimination, the final step.

options.t: The drug's first movement into systemic circulation
options.why: Absorption is the step that precedes distribution, not what happens during it.

questions.stem: What is biotransformation?
questions.why: Biotransformation is the chemical change a drug undergoes — usually in the liver — producing metabolites that prepare the drug for excretion.

options.t: The drug spreading out through the body's tissues
options.why: Spreading throughout body tissues describes distribution, a different step.

options.t: The kidneys filtering the drug out for excretion
options.why: Kidney filtering describes elimination, the step that follows biotransformation.

options.t: A chemical change the drug undergoes, typically in the liver
The drug's very first movement into the patient's systemic circulation
options.why: Movement into systemic circulation describes absorption, the first step.

questions.stem: Where are most drugs eliminated from the body?
questions.why: Most drugs are filtered through the kidneys during elimination, the fourth and final step of pharmacokinetics.

options.t: Exhaled through the lungs after hepatic breakdown
options.why: The lungs do clear volatile agents such as inhaled anesthetics, but the great majority of drugs leave through the kidneys.

options.t: Filtered mainly through the kidneys
Excreted in sweat and shed skin cells over several days
options.why: Sweat carries a trace of some drugs — enough to detect, nowhere near enough to matter for elimination.

options.t: Filtered mainly through the liver, and nowhere else
options.why: The liver is central to biotransformation, but elimination itself is primarily through the kidneys.

questions.stem: What is a drug's half-life?
questions.why: Half-life is the time it takes to metabolize or eliminate 50% of a substance from the plasma.

options.t: The time from administration to onset of effect
options.why: Time to onset of effect is a separate pharmacokinetic value, not the half-life.

options.t: The total overall time that the drug stays active in the body
options.why: Total active duration is a related but different concept from the specific half-life definition.

options.t: The time to clear half the drug from the plasma
The time between the first and second dose of a drug
options.why: Dosing interval is a clinical scheduling decision, not the definition of half-life itself.

questions.stem: What is the difference between pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics?
questions.why: Pharmacokinetics tracks what the body does to the drug (absorption through elimination, onset/peak/duration); pharmacodynamics tracks what the drug does to the body at the receptor level.

options.t: A term describing only a drug's onset of action
options.why: Pharmacokinetics covers onset, peak, and duration together — not onset alone.

options.t: Two completely different names describing one identical concept entirely
options.why: These describe two genuinely distinct halves of drug action, not the same concept twice.

options.t: A term that applies only to IV medications
options.why: Pharmacodynamics isn't restricted to any single route of administration.

options.t: What the body does to a drug, versus what it does back

questions.stem: What is an agonist medication?
questions.why: An agonist is a medication that initiates or alters cellular activity by binding to and activating a receptor.

options.t: A drug that works only by altering water balance
options.why: This isn't the general definition of an agonist — many agonists work through varied mechanisms, not just water balance.

options.t: A drug that starts or changes cellular activity
A drug with no effect on any cellular receptor
options.why: Agonists are defined precisely by their receptor effect, not an absence of one.

options.t: A drug that binds a receptor but blocks the response
options.why: Binding but blocking response describes an antagonist, the opposite action.

questions.stem: What does affinity refer to in pharmacology?
questions.why: Affinity is a medication's ability to bind with a particular receptor — a core concept in how agonists and antagonists work.

options.t: The specific route used to give the medication
options.why: Route of administration doesn't define a drug's affinity for a receptor.

options.t: The drug's brand name rather than its generic one
options.why: Naming convention has nothing to do with receptor affinity.

options.t: The overall total dose of drug that's administered
options.why: Total dose is a separate value from a drug's receptor-binding property.

options.t: A drug's ability to bind to a given receptor

questions.stem: What does potency describe?
questions.why: Potency is the concentration of medication needed for a cell response — as potency increases, the required dose decreases.

options.t: The overall total volume of drug contained in a given vial
options.why: Vial volume is a packaging detail, not the definition of potency.

options.t: The color coding printed on a medication's label
options.why: Label color coding isn't what potency refers to.

options.t: The drug concentration needed to produce a cell response
How recognizable a drug's brand name is to patients
options.why: Brand recognition has nothing to do with the pharmacologic concept of potency.

questions.stem: What is a competitive antagonist?
questions.why: A competitive antagonist temporarily binds receptor sites; its effect can be overcome by increasing the concentration of the competing agonist.

options.t: A drug that temporarily binds a receptor site and can be displaced
A drug that permanently binds receptors with no reversal
options.why: Permanent binding that can't be overcome describes a noncompetitive antagonist, the opposite type.

options.t: A medication that only works on gastrointestinal receptors
options.why: This isn't a receptor-site limited to GI action — competitive antagonism is a general pharmacologic mechanism.

options.t: A drug with absolutely no receptor interaction anywhere in the body
options.why: Competitive antagonists are defined by their receptor interaction, not an absence of one.

questions.stem: What is a noncompetitive antagonist?
questions.why: A noncompetitive antagonist permanently binds receptor sites, preventing activation — its effect can't be overcome by increasing the dose of the competing agonist, only by generating new receptor sites.

options.t: A term describing only medications given by the oral route
options.why: This mechanism isn't tied to any single route of administration.

options.t: Permanent binding that agonist can't overcome
A drug binding no receptors, with no measurable effect
options.why: A noncompetitive antagonist does produce a measurable, sustained receptor effect, not none at all.

options.t: Temporary receptor binding that more agonist can go on to displace
options.why: Temporary binding that can be displaced describes a competitive antagonist, the opposite type.

questions.stem: Naloxone is best described as what kind of drug relative to opioid receptors?
questions.why: Naloxone is an antagonist that competes with and displaces opioids at their receptor sites, reversing effects like respiratory depression — its efficacy is dose-dependent.

options.t: A drug that only works on beta-adrenergic receptors
options.why: Naloxone's target is the opioid receptor, not a beta-adrenergic one.

options.t: An agonist that further stimulates opioid receptors
options.why: An agonist would stimulate, not reverse, opioid receptor activity.

options.t: A drug with no effect on opioid receptors at all
options.why: Naloxone's entire mechanism is centered on opioid receptor interaction.

options.t: An antagonist that displaces opioids from receptors

questions.stem: Why does age affect a patient's response to medication?
questions.why: Body composition changes with age — children carry more water relative to body weight, and adults carry more fat — which affects how water-soluble versus fat-soluble drugs distribute.

options.t: Only patients past 65 show any age-related difference
options.why: This effect applies across the age spectrum, from pediatric through elderly, not just one group.

options.t: Age really has no measurable bearing on how any drug behaves at all
options.why: Age is explicitly listed as a factor affecting medication response, not an irrelevant one.

options.t: Age only matters for medications given by injection
options.why: This factor applies broadly across administration routes, not just injections.

options.t: Body composition shifts — more water in kids, more fat in adults

questions.stem: What does 'weight-based' dosing mean?
questions.why: Weight-based dosing multiplies the medication quantity by the patient's weight in kilograms, scaling the dose to the individual.

options.t: Dosing is scaled to height instead of to body weight
options.why: This describes a height-based, not weight-based, calculation.

options.t: The dose is scaled by multiplying it by the weight in kg
A standard dose adjusted up or down by body-mass index
options.why: BMI folds height back into the calculation. Weight-based dosing multiplies the dose by kilograms alone.

options.t: This kind of dosing is used only in pediatric patients
options.why: Weight-based dosing applies broadly, not exclusively to pediatric patients.

questions.stem: What is a therapeutic index?
questions.why: The therapeutic index describes the relationship between the median effective dose and the median lethal dose — a large difference means the drug is safer, a small difference means the patient must be closely monitored.

options.t: Relates the median effective dose to the median lethal dose
A drug's generic name held up against its brand name
options.why: Naming convention isn't what a therapeutic index describes.

options.t: The specific dose a physician orders for one patient
options.why: The physician-ordered dose is the desired dose, a distinct concept from the therapeutic index.

options.t: How long it takes for a drug to start working
options.why: Onset of action is a separate pharmacokinetic property, not the therapeutic index.

questions.stem: What is medication tolerance?
questions.why: Tolerance is a decreased efficacy of certain medications when taken repeatedly, resulting from receptor down-regulation.

options.t: The largest single dose considered safe for a patient
options.why: Maximum safe single dose is a different value from the concept of tolerance.

options.t: Reduced drug efficacy after repeated use, from down-regulation
An allergic reaction that happens right on the very first exposure
options.why: A first-exposure allergic reaction is a distinct immune-mediated response, not tolerance.

options.t: A dosing error that traces back to miscommunication
options.why: A miscommunication error is an administration mistake, unrelated to the tolerance concept.

questions.stem: What is an immune-mediated drug response?
questions.why: An immune-mediated response occurs in genetically predisposed patients who have an initial exposure and become sensitized to an allergen, setting up a reaction on subsequent exposure.

options.t: A reaction in genetically primed, sensitized patients
A term describing only topical medication reactions
options.why: This isn't limited to topical reactions — it describes a broader immune sensitization process.

options.t: A reaction that plays out in an identical way in every single patient
options.why: This response depends on individual genetic predisposition, not a universal reaction pattern.

options.t: A reaction driven only by dose, with no immune role
options.why: An immune-mediated response is, by definition, tied to immune function, not purely dose-driven.

questions.stem: What distinguishes an adverse medication effect from a side effect?
questions.why: Adverse medication effects are clinical changes that are unwanted and cause harm or discomfort, while side effects can be either useful or harmful depending on context.

options.t: Any effect the manufacturer did not list on the label
options.why: Adverse effects are well documented on labels — what defines them is that they are unwanted and cause harm.

options.t: Clinical changes that are unwanted and cause harm
Effects seen only with intravenous medications
options.why: This distinction isn't tied to a specific route of administration.

options.t: Effects that appear only after repeated dosing over time
options.why: Adverse effects can appear on a first dose. The distinction is harm, not how long the patient has been taking the drug.

questions.stem: Where are beta-1 receptors primarily located, and what happens when they're stimulated?
questions.why: Beta-1 receptors are concentrated in the heart and kidneys; stimulation increases inotropy, chronotropy, dromotropy, and vasodilation — remembered as '1 heart.'

options.t: Heart and kidneys — raises rate, conduction, and force
Peripheral arteries — stimulation constricts the vessels
options.why: Peripheral vasoconstriction describes alpha-1 receptor activity, not beta-1.

options.t: Lungs — receptor stimulation there opens the airway up wide
options.why: Bronchodilation from lung stimulation describes beta-2 receptor activity, not beta-1.

options.t: Brain — stimulation lowers the sympathetic response
options.why: Decreased sympathetic response from brain stimulation describes alpha-2 receptor activity.

questions.stem: Where are beta-2 receptors primarily located, and what happens when they're stimulated?
questions.why: Beta-2 receptors are found in the lungs, liver, GI tract, and blood, and their stimulation causes bronchodilation and vasodilation — remembered as '2 lungs.'

options.t: Peripheral arteries alone — stimulation constricts them
options.why: Peripheral vasoconstriction describes alpha-1 receptor activity, a different receptor entirely.

options.t: The brain alone — stimulation lowers sympathetic tone
options.why: Decreased sympathetic response from brain stimulation describes alpha-2 receptor activity, not beta-2.

options.t: Heart and kidneys — receptor stimulation there raises the heart rate
options.why: Increased heart rate from cardiac and renal stimulation describes beta-1 receptor activity, not beta-2.

options.t: Lungs, liver, GI, and vessels — dilates and opens up

questions.stem: What happens when alpha-1 receptors are stimulated?
questions.why: Alpha-1 receptors are located in the peripheral arteries, and their stimulation causes vasoconstriction.

options.t: Bronchodilation opening up the airway in the lungs
options.why: Bronchodilation describes beta-2 receptor stimulation, not alpha-1.

options.t: Lower sympathetic tone that brings blood pressure down
options.why: Decreased sympathetic response with lowered BP describes alpha-2 stimulation, a different receptor.

options.t: A faster heart rate along with stronger contractions
options.why: Increased heart rate and contractility describes beta-1 receptor stimulation, not alpha-1.

options.t: Vasoconstriction out in the peripheral arteries

questions.stem: What happens when alpha-2 receptors are stimulated?
questions.why: Alpha-2 receptors, located in the brain, decrease the sympathetic response and cause vasodilation when stimulated — lowering blood pressure, which is why alpha-2 agonists like clonidine treat hypertension.

options.t: A faster heart rate paired with stronger contractions
options.why: Increased heart rate and contractility describes beta-1 receptor stimulation, not alpha-2.

options.t: Lower sympathetic tone and dilation, dropping BP
Bronchodilation spreading through the lower airway
options.why: Bronchodilation is a beta-2 receptor effect, not alpha-2.

options.t: A higher sympathetic tone paired with peripheral vessel constriction
options.why: Increased sympathetic tone with vasoconstriction describes alpha-1 or general sympathetic stimulation, the opposite of alpha-2's effect.

questions.stem: Why is albuterol described as a selective beta-2 agonist while epinephrine is nonselective?
questions.why: Albuterol's selectivity for beta-2 receptors makes it useful for bronchodilation with less cardiac stimulation, while epinephrine's nonselective action on both beta-1 and beta-2 (and alpha) receptors produces broader effects.

options.t: Albuterol mainly hits beta-2; epinephrine hits beta-1 and beta-2
Albuterol is inhaled while epinephrine is injected
options.why: The route does differ, but selectivity is about which receptors the molecule binds, not how it gets there.

options.t: Epinephrine works on alpha receptors and albuterol on beta-1
options.why: Epinephrine hits alpha and beta both; albuterol's usefulness comes from favoring beta-2 over beta-1.

options.t: Albuterol blocks beta-1 while it stimulates beta-2
options.why: Albuterol does not block anything — it is a selective agonist, with weak beta-1 activity rather than blockade.

questions.stem: What do benzodiazepines do at the receptor level?
questions.why: Benzodiazepines enhance GABA receptor activity in the brain, producing antiseizure, anxiolytic, and sedative effects.

options.t: Boosting GABA activity in the brain to sedate the patient
Stimulating opioid receptors somewhere to relieve pain
options.why: Opioid receptor stimulation describes a narcotic, a different drug class.

options.t: Binding nicotinic receptors to trigger muscle contraction
options.why: Nicotinic receptor binding causing contraction describes a depolarizing paralytic, not a benzodiazepine.

options.t: Blocking acetylcholine receptors to halt movement entirely
options.why: Blocking acetylcholine to stop movement describes a paralytic agent, not a benzodiazepine.

questions.stem: How does a depolarizing paralytic like succinylcholine work?
questions.why: Succinylcholine activates nicotinic receptors, causing a brief burst of muscle twitching before quick-onset, short-acting paralysis.

options.t: Works purely on GABA receptors up in the brain
options.why: GABA receptor activity is the benzodiazepine mechanism, not the depolarizing paralytic's.

options.t: Activates nicotinic receptors, twitching then paralysis
Produces no effect at the neuromuscular junction at all
options.why: This drug class specifically targets the neuromuscular junction — the opposite of no effect there.

options.t: Permanently blocks nicotinic receptors, no initial twitch
options.why: Blocking with no initial activity describes a nondepolarizing paralytic, the opposite mechanism.

questions.stem: How does a nondepolarizing paralytic differ from succinylcholine?
questions.why: A nondepolarizing paralytic competes with acetylcholine at nicotinic receptor sites without activating them first, so there's no twitching phase — but it has a longer onset than succinylcholine.

options.t: Works only on GABA receptors, not the neuromuscular junction
options.why: GABA receptor action is a benzodiazepine mechanism, not how nondepolarizing paralytics work.

options.t: Causes the same initial twitching that succinylcholine does
options.why: Initial twitching is the depolarizing paralytic's signature effect, not the nondepolarizing type's.

options.t: Competes with ACh at nicotinic sites, no twitch phase
Has a shorter onset and duration than succinylcholine does
options.why: Nondepolarizing paralytics are described as having a longer onset, not a shorter one, compared to succinylcholine.

questions.stem: What distinguishes a selective from a nonselective beta-agonist medication?
questions.why: A selective beta-agonist like albuterol targets beta-2 receptors specifically, treating bronchospasm with less cardiac effect, while a nonselective one like epinephrine hits both beta-1 and beta-2.

options.t: There isn't really any distinction between these categories
options.why: A real and clinically meaningful distinction is described between these two categories.

options.t: Nonselective drugs work only down in the GI tract
options.why: Nonselective beta-agonists act on the cardiovascular and respiratory systems, not the GI tract specifically.

options.t: Selective hits beta-2 only; nonselective hits beta-1 and 2
Selective hits only alpha; nonselective hits only beta
options.why: This swaps the receptor families involved — selectivity here is about beta-2 versus both betas, not alpha versus beta.

questions.stem: What is the primary action of a corticosteroid in respiratory treatment?
questions.why: Corticosteroids reduce airway inflammation by acting as an immunosuppressant — a slower-onset but important part of treating conditions like asthma.

options.t: Relaxing bronchial smooth muscle directly within just seconds
options.why: Rapid direct muscle relaxation is the beta-agonist bronchodilator's role, not the corticosteroid's.

options.t: Reduces airway inflammation as an immunosuppressant
Blocks leukotrienes to head off bronchoconstriction
options.why: Blocking leukotrienes describes a leukotriene receptor antagonist, a different drug class.

options.t: Reverses respiratory depression caused by an opioid
options.why: Reversing opioid-induced respiratory depression describes naloxone's role, unrelated to corticosteroids.

questions.stem: What do histamine-2 receptor antagonists do?
questions.why: Histamine-2 receptor antagonists decrease acid production in the stomach, commonly used for GERD.

options.t: Cuts down on how much acid the stomach produces
Ramps up how much gastric acid gets secreted
options.why: Increasing acid secretion is the opposite of what an H2 blocker does.

options.t: Directly stimulates the body's vomiting center
options.why: Stimulating the vomiting center is the opposite of an antiemetic-adjacent GI drug's purpose.

options.t: Blocks opioid receptors somewhere up in the brain
options.why: Opioid receptor blockade is naloxone's mechanism, unrelated to H2 antagonists.

questions.stem: How do antiemetic medications generally work?
questions.why: Antiemetic medications act on receptors in both the brain and the GI tract to reduce nausea and vomiting.

options.t: Function by blocking nicotinic receptors at the junction
options.why: Blocking nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction describes a paralytic, unrelated to antiemetics.

options.t: Act on peripheral alpha receptors to slow gastric motility
options.why: Alpha receptors govern vascular tone. Antiemetics work on serotonin and dopamine receptors in the brainstem and the gut.

options.t: Act on brain and GI receptors to cut down nausea
Work only by directly neutralizing stomach acid
options.why: Acid neutralization describes an antacid, a different drug class than an antiemetic.

questions.stem: What is the mechanism of a Class I antidysrhythmic?
questions.why: Class I antidysrhythmics are sodium channel blockers — they slow sodium movement into cells, decreasing heart rate and depolarization of cardiac cells.

options.t: Beta-blockade that heads off a runaway high heart rate
options.why: Beta-blockade describes Class II, a different mechanism entirely.

options.t: Calcium channel blockade that slows rate and drops BP
options.why: Calcium channel blockade describes Class IV, not Class I.

options.t: Sodium channel blockade, slowing rate and depolarization
A longer refractory period aimed at treating tachycardia
options.why: Prolonging the refractory period describes Class III, not Class I.

questions.stem: What is the mechanism of a Class II antidysrhythmic?
questions.why: Class II antidysrhythmics are beta-adrenergic blocking agents — they inhibit catecholamine activation of beta receptors, preventing an excessively high heart rate.

options.t: A longer refractory period, prolonging the action potential
options.why: Prolonging the refractory period describes Class III, a different mechanism.

options.t: Sodium channel blockade slowing cellular depolarization
options.why: Sodium channel blockade describes Class I, not Class II.

options.t: Calcium channel blockade that lowers blood pressure
options.why: Calcium channel blockade describes Class IV, not Class II.

options.t: Beta-blockade that inhibits catecholamine activation

questions.stem: What is the mechanism of a Class IV antidysrhythmic?
questions.why: Class IV antidysrhythmics are calcium channel blockers — they displace calcium at certain sites, slowing heart rate, dropping chronotropy and dromotropy, raising inotropy, and lowering blood pressure.

options.t: Sodium channel blockade, slowing cellular depolarization
options.why: Sodium channel blockade describes Class I, a different mechanism than Class IV.

options.t: Beta-blockade, inhibiting catecholamine activation
options.why: Beta-adrenergic blockade describes Class II, not Class IV.

options.t: A longer refractory period aimed at tachycardias
options.why: Prolonging the refractory period describes Class III, not Class IV.

options.t: Calcium channel blockade, which slows rate and drops BP

questions.stem: What does adenosine do to cardiac conduction?
questions.why: Adenosine slows cardiac conduction through the AV node, producing a brief pause in cardiac activity — useful for terminating certain reentrant tachycardias.

options.t: Blocks calcium channels throughout the whole myocardium
options.why: Broad calcium channel blockade describes a Class IV drug, not adenosine's specific mechanism.

options.t: It actually speeds up conduction through the AV node instead
options.why: Speeding up AV conduction is the opposite of adenosine's actual effect.

options.t: It slows AV node conduction, briefly pausing cardiac activity
Acts as a long-acting beta blocker on the heart
options.why: Adenosine is notably short-acting, not a long-acting beta blocker.

questions.stem: What is a known adverse effect specifically associated with ACE inhibitors?
questions.why: ACE inhibitors alter the RAS system to decrease blood pressure and cardiac afterload, but carry a known risk of chronic dry cough and angioedema/facial swelling.

options.t: Reversible hearing loss and ringing in the ears
options.why: Ototoxicity belongs to aminoglycosides and high-dose salicylates, not to ACE inhibitors.

options.t: A chronic dry cough along with facial swelling
A persistent metallic taste with reduced appetite
options.why: Taste disturbance shows up with several drug classes, but the ACE inhibitor signature is a dry cough plus angioedema.

options.t: A rise in serum potassium from reduced aldosterone
options.why: This one is real but it is not the classic teaching point — the pairing that identifies an ACE inhibitor is dry cough with facial swelling.

questions.stem: What is a diuretic's general purpose in cardiovascular treatment?
questions.why: A diuretic corrects fluid overload — though it doesn't work well in a patient with kidney failure, since the kidneys are what the diuretic acts on.

options.t: Correcting a state of fluid overload somewhere in the body
Immediately relaxing bronchial smooth muscle
options.why: Bronchial smooth muscle relaxation describes a beta-agonist bronchodilator, not a diuretic.

options.t: Directly and immediately slowing down the patient's heart rate
options.why: Directly slowing heart rate describes a different drug class, like a beta blocker.

options.t: Blocking opioid receptors throughout the brain
options.why: Blocking opioid receptors describes naloxone, unrelated to a diuretic's purpose.

questions.stem: What is the difference between an antiplatelet drug and a fibrinolytic?
questions.why: An antiplatelet drug prevents new thrombus formation or extension of an existing one, while a fibrinolytic actively dissolves blood clots by breaking down fibrin.

options.t: Antiplatelet stops new clots; fibrinolytic dissolves old ones
This reverses it — antiplatelet dissolves, fibrinolytic prevents
options.why: This reverses the two mechanisms — dissolving clots is the fibrinolytic's job, not the antiplatelet's.

options.t: Both prevent clots, but only one is given intravenously
options.why: Route is not the distinction. One prevents a clot from forming or growing; the other breaks down fibrin in a clot already there.

options.t: Both dissolve clots, differing only in how fast they act
options.why: Only the fibrinolytic dissolves. An antiplatelet cannot break down a clot that has already formed.

questions.stem: Why does albuterol cause less tachycardia than epinephrine when treating bronchospasm?
questions.why: Albuterol is a selective beta-2 agonist, so it drives bronchodilation with relatively little beta-1 cardiac stimulation, while nonselective epinephrine hits both.

options.t: It selectively favors beta-2 over beta-1 receptors
It works through cholinergic rather than adrenergic sites
options.why: Its mechanism is adrenergic agonism, not a cholinergic pathway.

options.t: It blocks beta-1 receptors while opening the airway
options.why: Albuterol does not actively block cardiac beta-1 receptors.

options.t: It has no effect on any adrenergic receptor subtype
options.why: It plainly acts on adrenergic receptors, specifically the beta-2 subtype.

questions.stem: A heroin overdose patient improves after naloxone, then becomes somnolent again 40 minutes later. What best explains this?
questions.why: Naloxone competitively displaces opioids, but if it wears off while the longer-acting opioid is still present, the opioid re-occupies the receptors and symptoms return.

options.t: The opioid receptors were permanently destroyed
options.why: Receptors are not destroyed by either the opioid or its reversal agent.

options.t: The patient developed tolerance within the hour
options.why: Tolerance develops over repeated exposure, not within a single hour.

options.t: Naloxone's duration is shorter than the opioid's
Naloxone acts as a partial opioid agonist here
options.why: Naloxone is an antagonist at these receptors, not a partial agonist.

questions.stem: A medication has a narrow therapeutic index. What does this mean practically?
questions.why: A narrow therapeutic index means the median effective dose and the median lethal dose are close, so the patient must be monitored much more carefully.

options.t: The drug is unusually safe across a wide dose range
options.why: A wide margin between doses describes a large index, not a narrow one.

options.t: The effective and lethal doses sit close together
The drug works over only a narrow range of conditions
options.why: The index compares the effective dose against the lethal one — it is about the size of the safety margin, not the range of indications.

options.t: The drug only works when given intravenously
options.why: Therapeutic index describes dose margins, not route restrictions.

questions.stem: A drug slows the heart rate, reduces conduction speed, and lowers blood pressure by displacing calcium at its binding sites. Which class is it?
questions.why: Displacing calcium at its binding sites, slowing rate and conduction, and dropping blood pressure describes the Class IV calcium channel blockers.

options.t: Class II, the beta-adrenergic blockers
options.why: Class II works by blocking catecholamines at beta receptor sites.

options.t: Class IV, the calcium channel blockers
Class I, the sodium channel blockers
options.why: Class I acts on sodium movement and cellular depolarization instead.

options.t: Class III, which prolongs refractory period
options.why: Class III prolongs the refractory period rather than displacing calcium.

questions.stem: A patient on a long-term medication now needs a higher dose for the same effect, with no change in their disease. What explains this?
questions.why: Repeated exposure causes receptor down-regulation, so more drug is needed to produce the same cellular response — the definition of tolerance.

options.t: Tolerance from receptor down-regulation over time
An immune-mediated allergic response developing
options.why: An allergic response would produce symptoms, not a quiet loss of potency.

options.t: Reduced bioavailability caused by the dosing route
options.why: The route has not changed, so bioavailability is not the variable here.

options.t: A narrowing of the drug's therapeutic index
options.why: The therapeutic index is a fixed property, not something that shifts this way.

questions.stem: Why does a drug given orally generally produce a weaker effect than the same dose given IV?
questions.why: Bioavailability — how much drug actually reaches systemic circulation — is lower orally, since absorption through the digestive tract is slower and incomplete.

options.t: The oral route destroys receptor affinity
options.why: A route of administration does not alter receptor affinity itself.

options.t: The IV formulation is a more concentrated preparation
options.why: Concentration is about the volume it is dissolved in, not the dose delivered — the same milligram figure is being compared either way.

options.t: Oral drugs bind receptors less tightly
options.why: Receptor binding affinity is a property of the drug, not the route used.

options.t: Less of it reaches circulation intact
